set.text: Marisol Vega has been an epicure since childhood, when her grandmother taught her to taste the difference between real vanilla and the cheap imitation some bakers secretly use to adulterate cakes they sell as 'pure vanilla.' Now she writes a weekly food column, and last month she visited a tiny bakery on Fulton Street. The owner, a quiet man named Tomasz, served her a slice of plum tart so toothsome that she asked for the recipe on the spot. He only laughed and slipped a small almond cookie into her bag as lagniappe. Marisol is usually abstemious, skipping dessert most nights and drinking only water with dinner, but that afternoon she ate two slices and watched the regulars quaff strong coffee at the counter while they argued happily about football. Her column the next week was the warmest she had written all year.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “adulterate” mean?
options: decorate with extra layers of cream
bake for too long until dry
make richer by adding real vanilla
copy from another baker's recipe
sell at a higher price than usual
make worse by secretly mixing in something cheaper
qs.why: Some bakers secretly mix cheap imitation vanilla into cakes they sell as pure vanilla, which lowers their quality. It does not mean making them richer, which is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lagniappe” mean?
options: the payment for her tart
a sample she had asked to try
a polite thank-you note
an apology for slow service
a small extra gift given for free
a coupon for her next visit
qs.why: Tomasz slipped a free cookie into her bag on top of what she had; she had not asked for it or paid for it.

qs.q: Why was it unusual that Marisol ate two slices that afternoon?
options: Her doctor had told her never to eat sugar.
She normally eats and drinks very moderately and skips dessert.
She had disliked plum tart as a child.
The owner did not want to sell her a second slice.
She was planning to write a bad review.
She had never visited a bakery before.
qs.why: The passage says she is usually abstemious, skipping dessert and drinking only water, so two slices broke her normal habit.

why: Using imitation vanilla in one's own cake is not adulteration (no secret cheaper substitute in a product sold as something better); made the deception explicit to match the card and the keyed option. Fixed 'an apology for a slow service' grammar.

set.text: The bank's former treasurer, Gordon Pratt, was arraigned on a gray Monday morning and charged with taking nearly two million dollars from customer accounts. At his trial that autumn, his lawyer insisted the files would exculpate him, claiming a computer error had moved the money. On the witness stand, when the prosecutor asked where the funds had gone, Pratt prevaricated, talking about 'complex transfers' and 'timing issues' without ever giving a clear answer. Then the prosecutor revealed a darker detail: Pratt had tried to suborn a young clerk, offering her ten thousand dollars to tell the court she had made the transfers herself. The clerk refused and went straight to the police. Her recording of his phone call showed incontrovertibly that Pratt knew exactly what he was doing. By the end of the trial, the local paper was calling him 'the embezzler of Elm Street.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “prevaricated” mean?
options: admitted everything
refused to speak at all
spoke loudly and angrily
asked for more time to prepare
avoided a direct, honest answer by speaking vaguely
blamed his lawyer
qs.why: On the stand he talked about vague 'complex transfers' without a clear answer. He did speak, so 'refused to speak' is wrong.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “suborn” mean?
options: fire someone from her job
threaten someone with violence
hire someone as an honest witness
train someone to make bank transfers
protect someone from the police
secretly pay someone to do something illegal, such as lie in court
qs.why: He offered the clerk money to give false testimony, which is exactly this kind of illegal bribe.

qs.q: What showed beyond doubt that Pratt knew what he was doing?
options: A report proving a computer error moved the money.
The clerk admitting that she made the transfers.
His lawyer turning against him in court.
His own confession to the judge.
The clerk's recording of his call offering her money to lie.
An investigation by the local newspaper.
qs.why: The clerk's recording of his phone call showed incontrovertibly that he knew what he was doing. The computer-error story was only his lawyer's claim.

why: Procedure was wrong: an arraignment is a first appearance where the defendant is asked to plead, not questioned by the judge about where money went, and a trial does not follow within the same week. Moved the testimony to a later trial with the prosecutor asking on the witness stand; reworded the idea question, which claimed the call 'finally proved guilt' though no verdict is given.

set.text: For two centuries, the small island of Kestrel Rock suffered from the depredations of rats that had arrived on whaling ships. The rats ate seabird eggs by the thousands, and their baneful effect on the island's wildlife was plain: of eleven nesting species, only four remained. Some scientists feared the damage was irremediable. Then, in a five-year project, conservation workers set out to extirpate the rats completely, checking every cave and cliff for survivors. Visitors were also banned from certain beaches, since careless tourists had begun to despoil them with litter and broken glass. The work succeeded. Today, with the rats gone, the birds are returning, and the island's plants grow untrammeled across the hills. Several species once thought lost have nested there again, proving that some harm can be undone after all.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “extirpate” mean?
options: count and study them
remove them completely so that none are left
move them to another island
feed them to keep them away from nests
reduce their numbers slightly
keep them in cages
qs.why: Workers searched every cave and cliff for survivors, and the passage ends 'with the rats gone,' so the aim was total removal.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “untrammeled” mean?
options: in neat rows planted by workers
slowly and weakly
only inside protected fences
after being trampled by visitors
freely, without anything holding them back
with the help of fertilizer
qs.why: With the rats gone and visitors limited, plants spread freely. 'Trampled' only sounds similar.

qs.q: What do the returning birds show about the scientists' early fears?
options: The scientists were right that nothing could be done.
The damage was not as permanent as some had feared.
The rats were never really the problem.
Tourists caused more harm than the rats.
Only four species will ever nest there.
The birds came back before the rats were removed.
qs.why: Some scientists feared the harm could not be fixed, but the passage ends by saying it can be undone after all.

why: The extirpate 'why' quoted words ('the rats are gone') that are not in the passage.

set.text: Dear Clara, I write from the lighthouse on a stormy night, with a strange presentiment that the fishing boats will need our light more than usual. With the wind howling, I have felt disquieted all evening, and I cannot settle by the fire. The gulls cry plaintively outside the window, as though calling for someone who will not come. Father looks careworn these days; the long winters have added lines to his face, and he sleeps too little. Yesterday the harbor master came to forewarn us that a great storm was moving up the coast, so we have filled every lamp and checked every window. Still, I take comfort in Father's unfaltering courage. He has climbed those iron stairs every night for thirty years, and he says he will climb them tonight as well. Write soon. Your loving sister, Margit

qs.q: In the passage, what does “presentiment” mean?
options: a gift for the fishermen
an official report about the weather
a memory of an earlier storm
a written plan for the night
a promise made to her sister
a feeling that something is about to happen
qs.why: Margit senses that the boats will need the light more than usual; it is a feeling about what is coming, not a report or a memory.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “careworn” mean?
options: tired and sad after a long time of worry
very careful
angry and impatient
sick with a fever
dressed in old clothes
relaxed and carefree
qs.why: The lines on his face and his lack of sleep after long hard winters show long worry and strain.

qs.q: What does Margit find most comforting?
options: The harbor master's promise that the storm will miss them.
Her father's steady courage in doing his duty every night.
The sound of the gulls outside the window.
Sitting warm and calm beside the fire.
Knowing the fishing boats stayed in the harbor.
Her sister's plan to visit soon.
qs.why: She writes, 'I take comfort in Father's unfaltering courage,' then describes him climbing the stairs every night for thirty years.

why: 'disquieted' is taught as an adjective (feeling worried, uneasy); the passage used it as a transitive verb ('The wind has disquieted me'). Rewrote so it is used as the adjective on the card.

set.text: The college graduation party at the Patel house was meant to be a quiet dinner, but by nine o'clock it had turned almost bacchanalian. Cousins arrived from three cities, a neighbor brought a sound system, and someone hung flashing lights from every tree. Amid all the razzmatazz, the young graduates caroused in the backyard, clinking bottles of beer, singing loudly and dancing on the picnic table. Older relatives overindulged too, especially on Aunt Leela's famous sweets, which vanished within an hour. Only Ravi's grandfather, a doctor who had spent his career warning patients about intemperance, stayed calm and sipped his tea. When he finally asked everyone to lower the music at midnight, a few teenagers called him a spoilsport. He simply smiled, reminding them that the neighbors had to work in the morning, and the party ended peacefully soon after.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “razzmatazz” mean?
options: loud, flashy excitement and display
the quiet dinner
the famous sweets
a family argument
the cleanup afterward
the graduation ceremony
qs.why: The sound system and flashing lights in every tree are noisy, showy excitement.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “spoilsport” mean?
options: someone who is bad at sports
a doctor who treats athletes
someone who cheats at games
the loudest guest at a party
someone who ruins other people's fun
the person hosting the party
qs.why: The teenagers said this when he asked them to turn down the music, which ended part of their fun.

qs.q: Why does the grandfather's calm behavior fit his background?
options: He was the one who planned the party.
He had never liked music.
He was too tired to dance.
He was allergic to Aunt Leela's sweets.
He had spent his career warning people about a lack of self-control.
He wanted the neighbors to complain.
qs.why: As a doctor he warned patients about intemperance, so it fits that he stayed moderate while others overdid it.

why: 'carouse' and 'bacchanalian' on the cards both involve drinking alcohol, but the passage mentioned no drinking, so neither word was shown in its taught meaning. Added the adult graduates drinking beer.

set.text: In the last years of his life, the poet Yusuf Demir was nearly blind, so he dictated his work to an amanuensis, a young student named Selin who wrote down every word. Many of his poems mixed Turkish with old Persian phrases, and Selin had to transliterate the Persian words into Latin letters so that his publisher in Istanbul could read them. It was slow, delicate work, because a single careless mistake could garble a line beyond understanding. When tired, Yusuf also had a habit of eliding sounds and even whole small words, swallowing the ends of his phrases. At first this disconcerted Selin, who was never sure what he had meant. But her doggedness won out. Over three years she learned his voice so well that she could finish his sentences, and his final book was published with her name beside his.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “transliterate” mean?
options: translate the meaning into Turkish
copy neatly by hand
remove from the poem
read aloud to the publisher
write in a different alphabet, keeping the same sounds
explain in simple words
qs.why: She changed the Persian words into Latin letters so they could be read, not into Turkish meanings, which would be translating.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “disconcerted” mean?
options: made her feel uneasy and unsure
pleased her
made her angry
bored her
amused her
made her quit
qs.why: She was 'never sure what he had meant,' which left her uneasy and unsure how to proceed.

qs.q: What shows that Selin succeeded in her work?
options: She learned to read Persian before she met him.
She convinced him to stop dropping words.
She came to know his voice well enough to finish his sentences.
She wrote the final book on her own.
The publisher hired her to translate other poets.
She cured his failing eyesight.
qs.why: After three years she could finish his sentences, and her name was printed beside his on the final book.

why: The elide example used English ('I have been' -> 'I've been' -> 'been') for a Turkish poet dictating Turkish/Persian verse, which is not credible. Replaced with a language-neutral description of dropping sounds and small words.

set.text: Before the museum gala, Julian spent nearly an hour primping in front of the mirror, adjusting his silk scarf and polishing his shoes. His sister teased him for being foppish, but he insisted that tonight was important. At the gala, though, he was surprised by the guests. Many of the wealthiest people wore simple dark suits and plain dresses, without a single extra accoutrement. Meanwhile, a few other guests arrived covered in frippery: feathered hats, sparkling capes, gold-painted canes. The decorations followed the same pattern. The organizers had hung chintzy plastic chandeliers to save money, and the flashing lights around the stage seemed meretricious beside the quiet beauty of the paintings on the walls. On the way home, Julian took off his scarf, folded it carefully and decided that next time he would dress more simply.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “chintzy” mean?
options: cheap-looking and of poor quality
elegant and costly
covered in a flower pattern
very old and valuable
too bright to look at
borrowed from the museum
qs.why: They were plastic and bought 'to save money,' so they looked cheap. A flower pattern is a different meaning of a related word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “meretricious” mean?
options: deserving praise
dangerous
beautiful and calm
too dim to see
old-fashioned
showy but with no real value
qs.why: The flashing lights looked flashy and empty compared with the 'quiet beauty' of the paintings. It does not mean deserving merit.

qs.q: What did Julian seem to learn at the gala?
options: Only rich people should attend galas.
Silk scarves are no longer in fashion.
Museums should spend more on decorations.
Real elegance often looks simple rather than showy.
The guests in feathered hats were the best dressed.
His sister was wrong to tease him.
qs.why: He saw the wealthiest guests dressed plainly while showy outfits and lights looked cheap, and he decided to dress more simply.

why: 'The newest donors' arriving in gaudy frippery vs the wealthiest dressing plainly leans on the 'vulgar new money' class stereotype; made the showy guests unspecified and adjusted the matching idea option.

set.text: Every spring, Professor Oyelaran asks her first-year writing students to read aloud the worst sentence they wrote in high school. The results are always funny. One student read a poem of pure doggerel about her cat, rhyming 'cat' with 'hat,' 'mat' and 'that' six times. Another shared an essay so prolix that it took three pages to say that summer is hot. A third admitted to a sententious ending in which he warned readers that 'only those who respect their elders shall ever know true happiness.' The professor's favorite was a grandiloquent opening about 'the eternal, thundering ocean of human destiny,' followed immediately by the line 'and then I ate a sandwich,' a perfect case of bathos. 'Your early writing was jejune,' she tells them kindly, 'but that is how everyone begins.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sententious” mean?
options: angry and bitter
sad and tearful
full of very long sentences
preachy, as if lecturing others about right and wrong
funny and light
honest and modest
qs.why: The ending tells readers how to live in a self-righteous tone. 'Long sentences' is a careless guess from the look of the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bathos” mean?
options: a feeling of deep sadness
a long, boring section
a powerful, serious ending
a sudden, funny drop from something grand to something ordinary
a clever rhyme
a spelling mistake
qs.why: The grand 'ocean of human destiny' is followed at once by eating a sandwich, a comic fall from lofty to trivial.

qs.q: What is the professor's attitude toward her students' early writing?
options: She sees weak early writing as a normal stage, not something to be ashamed of.
She thinks students who wrote badly should leave the class.
She believes high school teachers did a terrible job.
She thinks poems are worse than essays.
She wants students to write the way they did in high school.
She is angry that the sentences are so bad.
qs.why: She speaks 'kindly' and says 'that is how everyone begins,' treating it as a normal starting point.

why: Sententious Q option 'short and wise' is a real (older) sense of sententious (pithy, full of maxims) and the example sentence is a short maxim, so it could be defended as correct. Replaced with a clearly wrong distractor.
